blocks.label: Block A — Pre-inflection core I (ledger ~items 55-210; weeks 3-5). One exemplar of every i-adjective final-vowel shape, plus first proof that a -i ending can be na-class.
items: 1. ii [1] — i — good / fine / OK. FROZEN LEXEME: carded citation-only (ii, ii desu, ii yo). Explicitly EXCLUDED from the stage-10 induction set (suppletive; see note on yoku/yokatta).
2. sugoi [2] — i — amazing / intense / extreme. Very high spoken frequency; also feeds the intensifier sugoku.
5. takai [2] — i — expensive. CARD 1 OF 2: price sense only, frame 'takai desu ne' over a price context. The height sense is card #47.
6. oishii [0] — i — tasty. (accent approximate: [0] per NHK; [3] is heard)
7. atsui [2] — i — hot (of the air OR of an object/liquid). Two kanji senses deliberately MERGED into one card; see note 12.
10. suki [2] — na — liked / fond of. First na-adjective, and deliberately one that ends in /i/.
11. genki [1] — na — well / energetic / in good spirits. Second /i/-final na-adjective.
12. daijoobu [3] — na — all right / fine / no problem.
blocks.rationale: These are the highest-frequency conversational adjectives, and between them they already cover all four i-adjective shapes: -ii (ii, ookii, oishii), -ai (chiisai, takai, hayai), -ui (atsui), -oi (sugoi, omoshiroi). Two of the three na-adjectives (suki, genki) end in the sound /i/, so from card 10 onward the learner has counter-evidence against the false rule 'ends in i = takes -katta' — before that rule has any chance to harden. daijoobu ends in -u and anchors the other end of the na class. ii is placed first because withholding the single most frequent adjective to protect an induction that does not open for eight more weeks is not a real trade; instead it is quarantined as an unanalyzed chunk.
blocks.interference: takai (#5) vs yasui (#31): 26 apart — required >=15, because both are [2], both 3-mora, both -ai, and both attach to prices. || takai (#5) vs hikui (#46): 41 apart, and takai's height sense is withheld entirely until #47, because takai has TWO antonyms and co-teaching either one early falsely narrows the sense. || atsui [2] (#7) vs samui (#17): 10 apart — required >=10; both temperature, both 3-mora, both accent [2], both -ui/-ui. Maximal interference pair in the set. || atsui [2] (#7) vs atsui [0] 'thick' (#48): 41 apart — required >=30, because in speech the ONLY distinguishing cue is the accent integer. || ookii (#3) vs ooi 'many' (#45): 42 apart — required >=25; one-mora difference, same initial long vowel. || suki (#10) vs sukunai (#44): 34 apart — shared /suk-/ onset. || hayai (#8) vs osoi (#50): 42 apart, antonym deliberately deferred.

blocks.label: Block B — Pre-inflection core II (ledger ~items 210-450; weeks 5-8). Bulks out each shape; adds the first Tier-A na-class trap.
items: 15. kawaii [3] — i — cute. (accent approximate: NHK [3]; colloquial [0] widespread)
17. samui [2] — i — cold (of the air / of how you feel).
18. furui [2] — i — old (of things, never of people).
21. ureshii [3] — i — glad / happy (about a specific thing).

22. yasashii [3] — i — kind, gentle. CARDED IN THE 'KIND' SENSE ONLY; the 'easy' sense is handed to kantan (#24), because spoken Japanese overwhelmingly uses kantan for 'easy' and the learner cannot see 優しい vs 易しい.
23. kirai [0] — na — disliked / hated. TIER-A TRAP: ends in the vowel hiatus -ai and is NOT an i-adjective. Predicted error *kiraikatta; correct kirai datta.
25. taihen [0] — na — tough, awful; also the intensifier 'very'.
blocks.rationale: Frequency ordering resumes, with two forced moves. First, kirai is pulled forward to #23 even though several later items outrank it, because it is the single most frequent Tier-A trap and the learner must meet it while the i/na distinction is still being actively built, not after the inflection rule has hardened. Second, furui is held to #18 rather than sitting next to atarashii, purely for rhyme separation from warui (#13). By the end of this block the running totals are 19 i-adjectives and 7 na-adjectives, so the na-class minimum (8) is one item short and the i-adjective minimum (12) is already cleared — the schedule is binding on the na side, not the i side, which is the opposite of the intuition.
blocks.interference: warui (#13) vs furui (#18): 5 apart — required >=4; shared -rui rhyme, identical accent [2], identical mora count. Semantically unrelated, so 4 is enough. || warui/furui vs karui (#49): 31/36 apart, completing the -rui triple separation. || samui (#17) vs tsumetai (#35): 18 apart. This gap is deliberate and its SECOND member is a discrimination card, not an acquisition card — see note 10. || kirai (#23) vs kiree (#37): 14 apart — required >=12. This is the worst pair in the whole adjective inventory for an audio-first learner: both na-class, both apply to people and things, near-minimal by ear (/kirai/ vs /kiree/), and distinguished by accent ([0] vs [1]). Both distinctions are exactly what the perception block trained, so this pair is where that block gets cashed in. || muzukashii (#16) vs kantan (#24): 8 apart — this is the real antonym pair (not muzukashii/yasashii), and 8 is close enough to read as contrastive without being a same-session collision. || tanoshii (#19) / ureshii (#21) / (later) kanashii (#56) / sabishii (#57): the -shii emotional cluster. 19 and 21 are 2 apart, which is tight; they are kept together because they are semantically NON-overlapping in the way that matters (tanoshii predicates an event, ureshii predicates the speaker) and that contrast is best taught adjacently. The two negative-valence members are exiled to Block E.

blocks.label: Block C — Induction set completion (ledger ~items 450-720; weeks 8-10). Everything here must be carded BEFORE stage 10 opens in week 11.
items: 31. hoshii [2] — i — wanted, want (a thing). Note it is an ADJECTIVE, not a verb, and it takes ga.
34. omoi [0] — i — heavy. Sole 'omoi' card; see note 13.
35. tsumetai [0] — i — cold to the touch (drinks, hands, objects, people's manner).
37. kiree [1] — na — pretty / clean / tidy. WRITTEN kiree, NOT kirei — see note 6.
blocks.rationale: This block exists to satisfy the induction thresholds on schedule, and its membership is chosen by shape gap, not by frequency. Coming into it the -oi and -ui shapes were the thin ones, so tsuyoi (#27), omoi (#34) and tooi (#36) are promoted above several more frequent candidates. At card #40 the standing totals are 29 i-adjectives and 11 na-adjectives; the -ui shape ends at exactly 4 exemplars (atsui, warui, furui, samui) and is the binding constraint on the entire schedule — if the ramp slips, this is the number that fails first, and the repair is to promote karui (#49) and nemui (#55). The four na-adjectives are back-loaded here so the last thing the learner sees before the inflection rule opens is fresh evidence that a whole class does NOT inflect.
blocks.interference: tsuyoi (#27) vs yowai (#54): 27 apart — required >=20. These are antonyms AND they share the mora /yo/ while differing only in what surrounds it; adjacency would be the worst decision in the list. This is the clearest case where the antonym-pair question resolves toward SEPARATE. || joozu (#38) vs heta (#39): ADJACENT ON PURPOSE — required separation zero. This is the clearest case resolving toward CO-TEACH: 3 morae vs 2, [3] vs [2], no shared segment, and they occur as a fixed conversational pair ('nihongo joozu desu ne' / 'iie, heta desu'). Nothing about them is confusable except that they are opposites, and opposition alone is not interference. || kiree (#37) vs kirai (#23): see Block B. || yasui (#30) vs takai (#5): 25 apart. || omoi (#34) vs omoshiroi (#9): 25 apart, shared /omo/ onset. || tsumetai (#35) vs samui (#17): 18 apart, deliberate — the #35 card is built AS a three-way discrimination card (samui / tsumetai / atsui) and depends on samui already being stable. || mijikai (#33) vs nagai (#20): 13 apart.

blocks.label: Block D — Post-inflection (ledger ~items 720-1000; weeks 11-13). The lexical -nai exception class, plus the accent-split and sense-split second cards that could not exist before the rule did.
items: 41. tsumaranai [3] — i — boring / dull. LEXICAL -nai: not a negative form. Negative is tsumaranakunai.
42. abunai [3] — i — dangerous / look out. LEXICAL -nai.
44. sukunai [3] — i — few / not much. LEXICAL -nai.
45. ooi [1] — i — many / a lot of.
46. hikui [2] — i — low (in height, in pitch, in a number).
47. takai [2] — i — tall / high. CARD 2 OF 2, height frame ('se ga takai', 'takai tatemono'). Same lemma and same accent as #5; split by collocation frame, not by accent.
48. atsui [0] — i — thick (a book, a wall, a coat). SEPARATE LEMMA from #7, distinguished in speech by accent alone. See note 12.
51. muri [1] — na — impossible / no way / can't be done.
52. dame [2] — na — no good / not allowed / broken.
blocks.rationale: Everything here is placed by dependency, not frequency — several of these items (abunai, sukunai, ooi, dame) outrank half of Block B on raw counts and are held back anyway. The four lexical -nai adjectives are the single most important scheduling decision in this list: put any of them in the pre-inflection set and the learner induces that -nai is part of the stem, or worse, meets tsumaranai in week 6 and back-forms a phantom positive *tsumaru-adjective. Held to week 11+, they instead become the productive first EXCEPTION to a rule that already exists, which is a card the learner can actually reason about — and they are carded as a labelled block of four precisely so the exception reads as closed rather than as evidence the rule is unreliable. #47 and #48 likewise cannot be taught before the learner has a stable single-sense takai and a stable single-accent atsui to contrast against.
blocks.interference: tsumaranai / abunai / kitanai / sukunai (#41-44) vs the ENTIRE -kunai negative paradigm from stage 10: this block must not open until the regular negative is at interval >=7 days, otherwise the exception contaminates the rule instead of the rule framing the exception. || sukunai (#44) vs ooi (#45): ADJACENT ON PURPOSE. Antonyms, but 4 morae [3] vs 3 morae [1] with no shared segment; and ooi's real interference risk is not sukunai at all, it is ookii. || ooi (#45) vs ookii (#3): 42 apart — required >=25. || hikui (#46) vs takai-height (#47): ADJACENT ON PURPOSE. The whole point of #47 is that it is a re-card, and pairing it with hikui is what makes the second sense audible as a distinct sense. || atsui-thick (#48) vs atsui-hot (#7): 41 apart. || karui (#49) vs omoi (#34): 15 apart — required >=12; antonyms, but the risk here is low (2-mora vs 3-mora, [0] vs [0], no shared segment) so the gap is modest. || karui (#49) vs warui (#13) / furui (#18): 36 / 31 apart, -rui cluster. || osoi (#50) vs hayai (#8): 42 apart.

blocks.label: Block E — Tail (ledger ~items 1000-1400; weeks 13-16). Where the frequency curve has already flattened and placement is nearly free.
items: 59. karai [2] — i — spicy-hot; salty (in some regions/uses).
60. akai [0] — i — red. SOLE COLOR ADJECTIVE in this list; see note 14.
62. yuumee [0] — na — famous. WRITTEN yuumee, NOT yuumei — see note 6.
blocks.rationale: By position ~50 the per-item token frequency has dropped to roughly a sixth of the block-A items and the differences between neighbors are inside the noise of any corpus estimate, so ordering here is driven almost entirely by interference distance and by semantic-set completion (a taste pair, an emotion pair, one color). This is also the honest boundary: nothing in this block is doing structural work, and the items immediately below the line are not meaningfully rarer than #60-63 — see note 15, which enumerates them rather than gesturing at them.
blocks.interference: yowai (#54) vs tsuyoi (#27): 27 apart, the required separation from Block C. || kanashii (#56) / sabishii (#57): ADJACENT ON PURPOSE, and this is the one adjacency in the list I am least sure about — 4 morae each, both [3], both -shii, both negative-affect, and the English glosses overlap in exactly the way that produces 'I know it's a sad one.' The defense is that they are syntactically distinct (kanashii predicates a situation, sabishii predicates the speaker's state) and that separating them only relocates the collision to tanoshii/ureshii. Fallback if the learner's lapse rate on either exceeds ~20 percent: push sabishii past #75. || kanashii (#56) / sabishii (#57) vs tanoshii (#19) / ureshii (#21): 35+ apart, the -shii cluster split across blocks. || amai (#58) vs umai: umai [2] 'tasty, skilful' is NOT in this list but will arrive from the noun/verb ledger; when it does, keep it >=15 from amai — one-mora difference, both about food. || karai (#59) vs kirai (#23): 36 apart — required >=25; /karai/ vs /kirai/ differ in one vowel, both 3 morae, and one is i-class while the other is the flagship Tier-A trap. Getting these two close together would undo the trap card. || akai (#60) vs the color NOUN aka: taught in different ledgers on purpose, see note 14.

notes: 1. INDUCTION REQUIREMENT, STATED AS A NUMBER (the question asked). i-adjectives: the MINIMUM to induce the four-slot paradigm (-ku, -kunai, -katta, -kute) rather than memorize it is 12, and 12 only works if it is 3 exemplars in each of the four final-vowel shapes -ai, -ii, -ui, -oi. A shape-unbalanced 20 is worse than a shape-balanced 12, because a learner whose exemplars are mostly -ai can induce the narrower and wrong rule 'the sequence a-i alternates with a-katta'. TARGET is 28 by adjective #40 (the schedule above delivers 29), for margin against lapses. The induction set must EXCLUDE ii (suppletive) and EXCLUDE all four lexical -nai adjectives. na-adjectives: MINIMUM 8, TARGET 11 (the schedule delivers 11 by #40). The number is not about morphology — na-adjectives have essentially none, they just suffix the copula — it is about inducing a CLASS BOUNDARY. Of those 8, at least 3 must end in the sound /i/ (this list uses suki #10, genki #11, kirai #23, benri #40) and at least 1 must be a Tier-A hiatus trap (kirai). Without those, the learner induces 'ends in i, therefore takes -katta' and the na class is learned as arbitrary lexical noise forever after.

2. THE FOUR-SHAPE COVERAGE, AUDITED AT CARD #40. -ai: chiisai, takai, hayai, itai, kowai, yasui, mijikai, tsumetai (8). -ii: ookii, oishii, atarashii, kawaii, muzukashii, tanoshii, ureshii, yasashii, isogashii, hoshii (10; ii itself excluded). -ui: atsui, warui, furui, samui (4 — THE BINDING CONSTRAINT). -oi: sugoi, omoshiroi, tsuyoi, omoi, tooi (5). Total 27 inducible + ii quarantined + 1 (nagai, -ai, miscounted above as needed) = 29 i-adjectives carded, 27-28 of them usable as induction evidence. If the ramp slips and -ui drops below 4, promote karui (#49) and nemui (#55) into Block C; those are the two cheapest repairs.

3. THE EXCEPTION LIST, ENUMERATED. The plan says 'about three'. It is not three, and the real list splits into tiers by how bad the trap actually is by EAR.

TIER A — genuine traps: citation form ends in a vowel-vowel hiatus -ai, phonologically indistinguishable in shape from a real i-adjective, but na-class. Predicted error is *X-katta / *X-kunai.
  kirai [0] — disliked (by far the most frequent; correct form kirai datta)
  shinpai [0] — worried (shi-N-pa-i; this one the brief did not list, and it is more frequent than three that it did)
  yakkai [0] (approx) — troublesome, a nuisance
  yukai [1] (approx) — pleasant, cheerful
  saiwai [0] — fortunate (also the adverb saiwai ni)
  aimai [0] — vague, ambiguous
  juudai [0] (approx) — serious, grave
That is 7, not 3. Note that only kirai and shinpai are frequent enough to make the core 63 — the rest sit at ledger positions 1500-4000, which means the trap deck is NOT a subset of the core adjective list and must be maintained as its own small deck that accretes members as the ledger advances.

TIER B — weaker traps: end in the sound /i/ but with a consonant onset on the final mora, so /suki/ not /sui/. Audible in principle, but English-ear learners generalize 'ends in -i' anyway, and *sukikatta is one of the most commonly attested beginner errors in the language.
  suki [2] — liked
  genki [1] — well, energetic
  benri [1] — convenient
  daiji [3] — important
  shoojiki [3] (approx) — honest

TIER C — NOT traps, listed only to close the set and stop the learner over-applying suspicion: joozu [3] (ends -u; no i-adjective ends in bare -u), heta [2] (-a), shizuka [1] (-a), daijoobu [3] (-u), kantan [0], taihen [0], muri [1], dame [2], hen [1], taisetsu [0], hima [0], raku [2].

REVERSE TRAP (i-adjectives that look na): ookii and chiisai have irregular attributive variants ookina and chiisana ('ookina koe', 'chiisana ko'). A learner who has just induced the na class will hear these and reclassify both words. Card the -na variants explicitly as frozen attributive-only alternates at stage 10+1, and state that they have NO other inflected forms — there is no *ookina datta.

4. THE HARD DIAGNOSTIC, WHICH IS WHAT THE EXCEPTION LIST BUYS. Once Tier A is closed and enumerated, the learner has a fully reliable ear rule, which a reader of kanji does not need but an audio-first learner absolutely does: a citation form whose last two vowels are in hiatus as ai / ii / ui / oi is an i-adjective, UNLESS it is on the Tier-A list. Everything else — every -ee, every -a, every -u, every -o, every consonant-plus-i — is na-class or a noun. The rule is only as good as the enumeration, which is the whole argument for enumerating it.

5. WHY -ee CANNOT BE AN i-ADJECTIVE, AND WHY THAT MATTERS HERE. There is no i-adjective in the language ending in the vowel sequence e+i. Zero. So the moment kirei is written as what it actually sounds like — kiree — the trap evaporates: /kiree/ cannot be an i-adjective by shape, and the learner needs no lexical exception at all. Same for teenee and yuumee. This is the single strongest argument for the doubled-long-vowel contract in the whole curriculum: it is not a transcription nicety, it converts a memorized exception into a derivable rule.

6. ROMANIZATION CONTRACT VIOLATIONS, FLAGGED. The plan writes obaasan, Tookyoo and kookoosee correctly, and then writes kirei, teinei and yuumei — which is the same ei->ee mapping it already applies inside kookoosee (sei -> see). Corrections: kirei -> KIREE [1]; teinei -> TEENEE [1] (accent approximate); yuumei -> YUUMEE [0]. The same fix propagates to the noun and verb ledgers wherever they have been written: sensei -> sensee, shitsurei -> shitsuree, eiga -> eega, keizai -> keezai, meishi -> meeshi, yotei -> yotee, benkyoo-sei -> -see, kirei ni -> kiree ni. The ONE place to keep two written vowels is where e and i sit across a morpheme boundary and are genuinely two morae: keito (ke + ito, 'wool yarn') stays keito, not *keeto. Rule for the TTS pipeline: within a morpheme, ei -> ee; across a compound seam, write both vowels. Since the learner never sees kanji, whichever spelling the deck ships IS the pronunciation they will produce — a card written 'kirei' will be produced as /ki-re-i/ with three distinct vowels, which is wrong and audibly foreign.

7. ii AND THE SUPPLETION — WHY IT DRILLS SEPARATELY. ii [1] is not merely irregular, it is defective: every inflected slot is filled from a different stem. yoku [1], yokatta [2], yokunai [2] (approx), yokute [2] (approx), yokereba, yosasoo. There is no *iikatta, *iikunai, *iikute, *iiku. Only the citation/attributive slot uses ii. Three reasons it must be quarantined from the induction set rather than just flagged inside it: (a) FREQUENCY DOMINANCE — ii is the most frequent adjective in conversation by a wide margin, so if it is in the induction set it is the exemplar the learner has the strongest trace of, and it teaches the wrong thing; (b) it is the ONLY suppletive adjective in the language, so its exceptionality is not informative about anything else; (c) it is not one item but a small productive sub-lexicon, because the suppletion is INHERITED by every compound built on it — kakkoii -> kakkoyokatta, kimochi ii -> kimochi yokatta, choodo ii -> choodo yokatta, tsugoo ga ii -> tsugoo ga yokatta, nakayoi -> nakayokatta. So the correct treatment is: card ii at #1 as a frozen citation-only lexeme; open a dedicated five-to-six-card micro-paradigm deck at stage 10 PLUS ONE WEEK, once the regular -katta/-kunai rule is at interval >=7 days; and drill the compounds in that same micro-deck so the stem swap is learned as a property of the yo-/ii lexeme family rather than as five unrelated irregular forms. SEPARATELY: yokatta as a bare interjection ('thank goodness / what a relief') is a distinct lexical item with its own very high frequency, and it should be carded as a frozen chunk in Block A or B, glossed as the interjection and NOT as 'was good'. It is not counted in the 63 above because it is an interjection card, not an adjective card — but omitting it from the ledger entirely would be a real gap.

8. ANTONYM PAIRS — THE ADJUDICATION RULE. Law 5 does cut both ways, and the resolution is that OPPOSITION IS NOT INTERFERENCE; FORM SIMILARITY IS. A pair should be CO-TAUGHT when the two members are phonologically distant (different mora count, different accent class, no shared onset or rhyme) and the pair is genuinely mutually defining. A pair must be SEPARATED when the members are phonologically close, because then the retrieval trace collapses to 'it's one of the temperature ones' and the learner recalls the domain instead of the word. A useful heuristic that reproduces every ruling below: separate if the two share accent integer AND mora count AND final shape.

9. THE SEVEN PAIRS, RULED. (a) atsui / samui — SEPARATE, minimum 10, actual 10. Both 3 morae, both [2], both -ui, same semantic field. Worst-case profile on every axis. (b) atsui / tsumetai — CO-TEACH, but the pairing is misconceived: these are not antonyms of each other in the way that matters. The learner's actual error is saying samui about a cold drink. So the real contrast to teach is samui vs tsumetai (state of the ambient air / state of the touched object), with atsui as the shared hot term that covers both domains and therefore needs no split. Hence the #35 card is built as a three-way discrimination card, placed 18 after samui so it trains discrimination on an already-stable item rather than causing acquisition interference. (c) ookii / chiisai — CO-TEACH, adjacent at #3/#4. Both [3] and both 4 morae, which by the heuristic is two of three strikes, but segmentally they share nothing (/oo-kii/ vs /chii-sai/), they are maximally concrete, and there is no third competitor to collapse into. (d) takai / yasui — SEPARATE, minimum 15, actual 25. Both [2], both 3 morae, both -ai, both attach to prices: all three strikes. (e) takai / hikui — CO-TEACH, adjacent at #46/#47, but ONLY at the second takai card. This is the consequence of takai having TWO antonyms: yasui for price, hikui for height. Co-teaching either one at #5 would silently teach the learner that takai means only the one sense. So takai gets two cards, split by collocation frame (not by accent — both senses are [2]), with the price sense alone in Block A and the height sense re-carded against hikui in Block D. (f) atarashii / furui — CO-TEACH in principle (5 morae [4] vs 3 morae [2], nothing shared), and they sit 4 apart at #14/#18 only because furui had to clear warui's rhyme. Also flag the asymmetry: furui does not apply to people, so 'he is old' is toshiue / toshiyori, not *furui hito. (g) omoshiroi / tsumaranai — SEPARATE, and NOT for antonymy. tsumaranai's interference is with the negative INFLECTION, not with omoshiroi, so it is held to #41 as part of the lexical -nai block. The gap ends up 32, but the governing reason is morphological scheduling. Also (h), added: tsuyoi / yowai — SEPARATE, minimum 20, actual 27; shared /yo/ mora, both [2], both 3 morae. (i) joozu / heta — CO-TEACH, adjacent, zero separation; the clearest co-teach in the list.

10. atsui, VERIFIED (the question asked for verification, and the plan's claim checks out). Standard Tokyo accents: 暑い (hot air) atsui [2]; 熱い (hot object/liquid, also 'passionate') atsui [2]; 厚い (thick) atsui [0]. So the plan is correct that there are two [2] senses and one [0] sense. FINAL CARD TREATMENT: (i) MERGE the two [2] senses into ONE card at #7, glossed 'hot — of the air or of an object'. They are the same phonological word with the same accent and the same class; the air/object split is fully recoverable from context and is not a listening problem, so splitting them would create two cards with identical audio, which is the definition of a bad card. (ii) SPLIT 厚い as a separate lemma at #48 with accent [0]. In speech the ONLY cue distinguishing it is the accent, which makes this the highest-value pitch-accent payoff card in the entire adjective set, and it must be recorded in frames where the accent is actually realized and contrastable: 'atsui ocha' (head-accented pattern) against 'atsui hon' (flat pattern). (iii) RISK NOTE: 厚い is not frequent in conversation, and if the learner's accent discrimination is not reliable by week 12 the safe fallback is to demote #48 from a bare-word card to a pure collocation card (atsui hon / atsui kabe / atsui kooto), accepting that the accent contrast is carried implicitly by the frame rather than tested directly.

11. omoi, VERIFIED — and the plan's 'same for omoi' is only half right. Accents: 重い (heavy) omoi [0]; 思い (thought, feeling) omoi [2]. So the [0]/[2] contrast is real, but the [2] member is a NOUN, not an adjective, which means there is no sense-split to make inside the adjective at all. FINAL CARD TREATMENT: 重い omoi [0] is carded once, at #34, as the sole 'omoi' in the first 1,000 items, and it is not split — the 'burdensome / serious' extension (omoi byooki, omoi kimochi) is a collocation that comes free and needs no card. 思い [2] is EXCLUDED rather than split; its genuinely useful derivative is omoide [0] 'memory', which is phonologically distinct and belongs in the noun ledger. There is a third collision the plan did not name: omoi- is also the i-stem of omou 'think' (omoimasu), so 'omoi' as a bare string is adjective, noun, and verb stem at once. That collision is largely neutralized by the contraction-citation contract, since the learner meets omotteru and omotta rather than a bare omoi-, but the verb ledger should still keep omoimasu at least 15 positions from #34.

12. THE ORDERING VARIABLE'S ONE FAILURE MODE, STATED HONESTLY. Front-loading shape coverage means several genuinely frequent items (abunai, sukunai, ooi, dame, hikui) sit 30-40 positions later than raw frequency would put them, so for roughly weeks 6-11 the learner has a slightly unnatural adjective vocabulary — strong on the four shapes, thin on high-frequency negatives. The trade is accepted because the cost is a few weeks of mild under-coverage against the benefit of an inflection rule that is induced rather than memorized, and induced rules generalize to the 200 adjectives that are never carded at all. If that trade turns out to feel bad in practice, the cheapest partial reversal is to move ooi and dame into Block B, which costs nothing structurally.

13. COLORS ARE MOSTLY NOT ADJECTIVE CARDS. Only akai (#60) appears here, deliberately. In conversation the dominant form of a color word is the BARE NOUN — aka, shiro, kuro, ao, kiiro — because colors most often appear as one-word answers, as attributives with no ('aka no kuruma'), and in compounds. The i-adjective forms akai / shiroi / kuroi / aoi / kiiroi are real but secondary. So the color set belongs in the noun ledger, and akai is carded here as the single anchor that teaches the derivational pattern 'color noun + i = color adjective', from which the other four are free. This also avoids five near-identical [2]-accented -oi/-ai cards landing in the same block, which would be a self-inflicted interference cluster. Keep akai at least 15 positions from the noun aka in the combined ledger.

14. WHAT IS IMMEDIATELY BELOW THE LINE, ENUMERATED — because 'the tail is short' is only a defensible claim if the boundary is shown rather than asserted. Adjectives 64-85, approximately, in rough order: atatakai [4] (warm; contracted attakai [3] is the citation form under the contraction contract), suzushii [3] (cool/pleasant), chikai [2] (near), hidoi [2] (awful), kibishii [3] (strict), utsukushii [4] (beautiful), mazui [2] (bad-tasting), erai [2] (impressive/tough), kuroi [2], shiroi [2], aoi [2], kiiroi [0], tsurai [2] (approx; hard to bear), urusai [3] (noisy/annoying), shinpai [0] na (worried — a Tier-A trap, so it is drilled in the trap deck earlier than its frequency rank), iroiro [0] na, shinsetsu [1] na, anzen [0] na, jiyuu [2] na, hitsuyoo [0] na, raku [2] na, hima [0] na, daiji [3] na, rippa [0] na, fuben [1] na, tokubetsu [0] na, teenee [1] na (approx). The point of listing these: the frequency drop from #60 to #85 is small — perhaps a factor of two — whereas over the same 25-item span in the noun ledger it is far steeper. That is the empirical content of 'adjectives have a shorter tail', and it is why the ordering variable for adjectives can afford to be dominated by induction structure rather than by frequency, which would be an indefensible choice for nouns.

16. ONE THING THAT SURPRISED ME. Going in, the obvious assumption was that the i-adjective count would be the binding constraint on when inflection can open. It is not, and it is not close — 12 shape-balanced i-adjectives arrive by roughly card #22, well inside week 7. The binding constraint is the NA-adjective count, and specifically the requirement for at least three na-adjectives ending in the sound /i/, because those are the only cards that carry negative evidence against the false rule the learner is otherwise guaranteed to induce. That inverts the natural instinct, which is to treat na-adjectives as the easy class that can be added whenever — they are the easy class morphologically and the hard class classificationally, and for an audio-first learner only the second kind of difficulty exists.
orderingVariable: Position in the stage-10 induction schedule, not raw frequency. Formally, the sort key is a three-level lexicographic function: (1) HARD GATE — the induction set must be complete by adjective #40, which lands in week 10, one week before i-adjective inflection opens. 'Complete' is defined numerically: at least 28 i-adjectives carded with at least 4 exemplars in EACH of the four final-vowel shapes (-ai, -ii, -ui, -oi), and at least 10 na-adjectives carded of which at least 3 end in the sound /i/ and at least 1 is a Tier-A hiatus trap. Items are promoted or demoted to satisfy this gate. (2) DEPENDENCY — items whose card cannot be authored until a rule exists (the lexical -nai class; the accent-split atsui [0]; the second-sense takai) are held to Block D regardless of frequency. (3) TIEBREAK — descending conversational token frequency, CEJC-like, approximate. Then a final pass applies interference separation as a local shuffle of at most plus-or-minus 10 positions, which never violates the gate because the gate is checked at a block boundary rather than per item.
whyThatVariable: The obvious alternative is pure descending conversational frequency, and it fails here for a reason that does not apply to the noun ledger: the adjective tail is short, so frequency stops discriminating almost immediately. Roughly (approximate, from spoken-corpus counts), the top 60 adjectives cover something like 85-90 percent of all adjective tokens in conversation, and the token ratio between rank 10 and rank 60 is on the order of 6:1 — whereas across the same span in the noun ledger it is well over 100:1. Past about rank 15 the frequency differences between neighbors are inside the error bars of any corpus estimate, so ordering by frequency there is ordering by noise. That leaves the ordering with exactly one degree of freedom worth spending, and the highest-value thing to spend it on is guaranteeing that the inflection rule can be INDUCED on schedule rather than memorized — which requires shape balance, not frequency rank. Pure frequency actively sabotages this in two specific ways. First, it under-supplies the -ui shape, which is the rarest of the four among high-frequency adjectives and which this schedule barely clears at 4 exemplars; a frequency-only order can easily reach week 11 with two. Second, and worse, it places the lexical -nai adjectives early — abunai, sukunai and tsumaranai are all frequent enough for the top 30 — which teaches the learner a phantom -nai stem weeks before the real negative rule exists, and poisons the induction the whole schedule is built to protect. A third, smaller reason: frequency counts merge homographs, so a frequency-driven list silently hands you one 'atsui' and one 'takai' entry when the audio-first learner needs two of one (split by accent) and two of the other (split by collocation frame), a distinction only a hand-built ledger can make.
